overview: This 106-page State Department file documents U.S. diplomatic and naval-intelligence monitoring of Japanese activities in Ecuador from 1932 to 1939. Its correspondence follows Japanese immigration, fishing and alleged reconnaissance near the strategically significant Galápagos Islands, disputed claims of intimidation and espionage, reports of unidentified submarines, and a later Japanese agreement to develop Ecuadorian cinchona and quinine production. Much of the file consists of Japanese propaganda circulated in Guayaquil—especially the pamphlet How the North China Affair Arose—which justified Japan’s actions in China by blaming Chinese nationalism, militarism, Communism, and the Nanjing government. Taken together, the documents show how commercial ventures, migration, maritime activity, propaganda, and strategic anxieties became intertwined in U.S. assessments of Japanese influence in Latin America.
interest: Shows prewar U.S. suspicion of Japanese activity in the eastern Pacific, with Japanese advocacy alongside.
